title: Sharing and Publishing Your Writing
keyIdea: Writing is for readers and listeners. When you read your own writing aloud, be clear and loud enough for the back row, pause at full stops, question marks and exclamation marks, and let your voice show the meaning. To publish, you make a neat final copy after you edit, often by typing it: Shift for capital letters, the space bar between words, Backspace to delete.

kid: When you share your writing, you read it out to other people. Stand up tall and hold the page low, so it does not hide your face. Be clear and loud, so the back row can hear you. Do not shout.
The marks in your writing tell you how to read it. Pause at a full stop. At a question mark, like Can I come too?, your voice goes up. At an exclamation mark, say it with a strong voice.
Look up at the people now and then. Read at a steady speed, not too fast. If you trip on a word, stop, go back and read it again.

To publish means to make a best copy for readers. You plan, draft and edit first. Then you can type it. Hold Shift to make a capital letter. Press the space bar between words. Press Backspace to take away a letter.
adult: This topic follows the national curriculum for England. In Year 1, pupils read their writing aloud clearly enough to be heard by peers and the teacher. In Year 2 they use the right intonation to make the meaning clear. In Years 3 and 4 they read to a group or the class and control tone and volume. In Years 5 and 6 they perform their own compositions with intonation, volume and movement. The US Common Core adds digital tools to produce and publish writing, and keyboarding skills from Grade 3 onward.

Useful terms: audience, volume, intonation, tone, pace, punctuation, draft, edit, final copy, publish, and keyboarding words such as Shift key, space bar and Backspace. Punctuation is a reading map: a full stop means pause, and a question mark or exclamation mark changes the tune. A yes or no question usually rises at the end. A question that starts with what or where often falls.

Common mistakes: reading to the page instead of the room, so the voice drops; racing past full stops; shouting instead of projecting; a flat voice that hides questions and jokes; and publishing a first draft before it is edited. When typing, children often press a letter harder for a capital, run words together, or forget the final full stop. Be careful to praise a clear voice and a fixed slip, not just a neat page.

In the lab your child turns a voice dial until all four rows hear, without the front row covering their ears. They tap the three pauses in a short beach story, match three sentences to their tune, press the key that fixes four typed lines, and put plan, draft, edit, publish and share in order.

familyTip: At bedtime, swap roles: your child reads you something they wrote. Sit at the far end of the room and give a thumbs up when you can hear every word.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: turn your voice up so the back row hears, pause at the marks, give each sentence its tune, fix typed lines with the right key, then publish.

practice.prompt: You are reading your story to the whole class. How should you speak?
choices: Clear and loud, so the back row hears
practice.hint: Think of the person at the very back of the room.
practice.explain: Clear and loud lets the back row hear. A whisper is too quiet and shouting is too much.

practice.prompt: Your story has {a} sentences. Each one ends with a full stop. How many times do you pause at a full stop when you read it all?
practice.hint: There is one full stop at the end of each sentence.
practice.explain: {a} sentences have {a} full stops, so you pause {a} times.

practice.prompt: How does your voice go at the end of “Do you like frogs?”
practice.hint: It is a question you answer with yes or no.
practice.explain: A yes or no question goes up at the end, so the listener knows you are asking.

practice.prompt: You typed a sentence with {w} words. How many times did you press the space bar between the words?
practice.hint: A space goes between two words, not before the first one or after the last.
practice.explain: {w} words have {=w-1} gaps between them, so you press the space bar {=w-1} times.

pool.prompt: Which key do you hold to type a capital letter?
pool.hint: It is the key with an arrow pointing up.
pool.explain: Hold Shift and press a letter to make it a capital.

pool.prompt: When should you publish your writing?
choices: Straight after you make a plan
pool.hint: Publishing is the best copy that readers see.
pool.explain: You publish after you plan, draft and edit, so readers get your best copy.

pool.prompt: You read “Look out, a shark!” to the class. How should it sound?
pool.hint: Look at the mark at the end.
pool.explain: The exclamation mark shows a strong feeling, so say it with a strong voice.

pool.prompt: You trip on a word while reading aloud. What is best?
choices: Go back and read it again
Skip the rest of the story
pool.hint: Your listeners want to know what the sentence says.
pool.explain: Going back and reading it again fixes the slip, and the story still makes sense.

pool.prompt: You typed a word with {n} extra letters on the end, and the cursor is just after them. How many times do you press Backspace?
pool.hint: Each press of Backspace deletes one letter just before the cursor.
pool.explain: Each press deletes one extra letter, so you press Backspace {n} times.

pool.prompt: Why should you hold your page low when you read aloud?
choices: So it does not hide your face and voice
So no one sees your writing
pool.hint: Where does your voice need to go?
pool.explain: A low page keeps your face and voice clear for the listeners.

pool.prompt: Your story has {q} question marks and {e} exclamation marks. At how many of these marks does your voice change its tune?
pool.hint: Both a question mark and an exclamation mark change how your voice sounds.
pool.explain: {q} question marks and {e} exclamation marks make {=q+e} places where your voice changes.

pool.prompt: You typed “Icanswim.” What do you need to add?
pool.hint: Can you see where one word ends and the next starts?
pool.explain: Press the space bar between the words: I can swim.
